summary: This Neighborhood Stories piece, dated September 10, 2023, examines how rising interest rates are reshaping the local housing market. It covers higher homeownership costs, rising rents, slowed new construction, a resilient luxury segment, and gentrification concerns, using quotes from local residents and professionals. It closes with policy discussions such as zoning changes, housing subsidies and first-time buyer support.
one_line: A local look at how rising interest rates affect home buying, rents, construction, luxury sales and neighborhood character.
key_facts: The article is dated September 10, 2023, yet it cites comments from later dates in September and October.
Real estate expert Thomas Greenway said on September 20 that interest rates "are the heartbeat of the market" and a minor uptick can decide whether a buyer enters or waits.
Rebecca Lui, a teacher at the local high school, has saved for years to buy a home but is unsure she can afford a mortgage after the recent spike in interest rates.
Rising interest rates have also hurt existing homeowners who want to refinance, not only new buyers.
Slowing home purchases have raised demand for rental properties and pushed rental prices up, as buyers priced out of ownership turn to long-term renting.
Jason Flemming, a property owner with several rental units, said on October 5 that he is seeing higher demand and an inevitable increase in rental prices.
Higher rents are pushing some residents toward the outskirts of the neighborhood or into shared living arrangements.
City planner Harold Jenkins said in mid-September that developers are cautious and a few projects have been delayed.
Clarisse Fontaine, a high-end real estate agent, said on October 12 that the luxury market is resilient and clients are still closing deals, with a bit more negotiation.
Wealthier buyers rely less on mortgage financing, so the luxury segment is less sensitive to interest rate changes.
Community leader Marcus Yee warned on September 27 of losing neighborhood diversity as 'For Sale' signs go up, a process linked to gentrification.
Financial advisor Anita Desai suggested on October 7 that worried residents seek counsel on strategies to mitigate rising costs.
Policy discussions on zoning changes, housing subsidies and first-time homebuyer support are gaining traction, with frequent town hall meetings.
